## Design

### 2026-09-30 — I started with a simple idea: an Arduino that sounds a buzzer when water leaks from a pipe. I asked for a parts list, then checked which programming language and editor I'd use, and found out it's C++

**2h**

I started with a simple idea: an Arduino that sounds a buzzer when water leaks from a pipe. I asked for a parts list, then checked which programming language and editor I'd use, and found out it's C++ and that either the Arduino IDE or VS Code with PlatformIO would work. After that,

![image_2026-09-30_202224210](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/ZB18468vV6xymMeGfUgN9PiGVu6vR4in/b3930d37fe97e7ed6947ad92ca7f5053f63abac3c5a64dcbca102b65c6801ace.png)

 I went through the actual listings one at a time and checked each against the project. The water leak sensor with the 3.5mm plug turned out to be two bare probes on a cable, which suits the job because I can put them under a pipe while the board stays dry. Since the Uno has no 3.5mm socket, I learned I needed a breakout board and compared a screw-terminal one with the CJMCU TRRS one. I confirmed the ATmega328P Uno R3 clone runs the same code as the official board, and that the 400-point breadboard has plenty of room for the buzzer and wiring. The only thing still on my list is a pack of male-to-male jumper wires, which none of those listings clearly include.

![image_2026-09-30_202303809](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/ZB18468vV6xymMeGfUgN9PiGVu6vR4in/535cc22a79e96ead7e84ee725b019955795db19bfaa9cecf1b8cb59a35436688.png)

### 2026-10-01 — ![image_2026-10-01_172500317](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/ZB18468vV6xymMeGfUgN9PiGVu6vR4in/94c557c8d92fd5b9c916ec75f9d097913b1d9e7eef3cf26608eb888576abe3c6.png)

**3h**

![image_2026-10-01_172500317](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/ZB18468vV6xymMeGfUgN9PiGVu6vR4in/94c557c8d92fd5b9c916ec75f9d097913b1d9e7eef3cf26608eb888576abe3c6.png)

![image_2026-10-01_172441571](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/ZB18468vV6xymMeGfUgN9PiGVu6vR4in/0254f7335e9516d07ede76511eb940a5b3b646e248bc21972586e0671218f3d1.png)
/human

I wrote the code in C++ for the Arduino IDE, and it's short. At the top, I named the two pins I'm using: pin 2 for the water sensor and pin 8 for the buzzer, so I can change them later in one place. In setup(), I set the sensor pin to INPUT_PULLUP, which means the pin reads HIGH while the probes are dry and drops to LOW as soon as water connects them to ground. That also meant I didn't need an extra resistor. I set the buzzer pin as an output. In loop(), the board checks the sensor over and over. If the pin reads LOW, it turns the buzzer on for 300 milliseconds, off for 300 milliseconds

![image_2026-10-01_172357374](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/ZB18468vV6xymMeGfUgN9PiGVu6vR4in/33d144eae342180c6cf1555aa9e627e0498979701a8e7bcd5e3813ff5c9fe68b.png)

, and repeats, so it beeps for as long as there's water. If the pin reads HIGH, it keeps the buzzer off. To test it, I upload the sketch and touch the two probes together or dip them in a little water, and the buzzer should start beeping.
